title: The Story of the Hermit
excerpt: (The original text appears in the Chronological Autobiography of Master Hanshan Deqing.)

inline.s: (The original text appears in the Chronological Autobiography of Master Hanshan Deqing.)
One day, Master Hanshan Deqing journeyed to Panshan
(a famous mountain northwest of the town of Jixian in Tianjin, an offshoot of the Yan Mountains and the renowned mountain east of Beijing, praised as “the foremost mountain east of the capital”)

Qianxiang Peak. When he reached the summit of Panshan, he saw a hermit dwelling beside the rocky crags near the top, with grey hair and an earthy complexion. The Master went in and made obeisance to him, but the hermit did not even raise his head, simply sitting upright with concentrated mind. Whatever the Master asked him, he did not utter a sound. Realizing that this hermit was no ordinary man, the Master sat down beside him and began to meditate.

After a while the hermit rose to boil tea, and when it was ready poured himself a cup and drank. Seeing this, the Master also took a cup and drank. When the tea was finished, the hermit put the tea things back in their place and silently sat in meditation once more; the Master did likewise. After another while, the hermit rose to cook a meal, and when it was ready filled a bowl and ate by himself; the Master likewise filled a bowl and ate with him. After the meal, the hermit again sat upright as before, and the Master followed his example. When night fell, the hermit rose and went outside the crag to do walking meditation, and the Master also went out to walk.

On the second day, the hermit no longer stirred. The Master, following the hermit's usual times for tea and meals, boiled tea and cooked at the proper hours; after the two had eaten, they again sat in quiet meditation and investigation, and at nightfall went out to walk together. Thus they passed seven days in utter silence, after which the hermit at last opened his mouth and asked the Master:
Where have you come from?”
From the south.”
What have you come here to do?”
I came especially to visit the hermit.”
The hermit's appearance is so ordinary — there is nothing special about it at all?”
I saw through it the moment I entered the door!”
Hearing this, the hermit laughed and said: “I have lived here for more than thirty years, and only today have I met a kindred spirit
(a person of the same style)
!” So he invited the Master to stay, and the Master, feeling that he had met a superior adept from whom he could well learn, also stayed on.

One night the Master went as usual to walk before the crag. As he walked, suddenly a thunderous sound erupted at the crown of his head, like a bursting clap of thunder. In an instant, mountains, rivers, and the great earth — the whole world of body and mind — abruptly became empty. This emptiness was not the “emptiness” of the eye faculty set against the dust of emptiness, but a state of empty samādhi in accord with the mind. The Master remained in this empty samādhi for about the time it takes a five-inch stick of incense to burn before he slowly began to feel the presence of his body, then slowly felt the solidity of the earth beneath his feet, and, opening his eyes, slowly saw the mountains, rivers, and great earth once more. All the physiological functions of his body returned to their former state. His body felt as though borne up by a breeze — light and joyful — and the inner experience was beyond all description.

When the Master returned to the crag, the hermit asked him: “Why did your walking tonight last so long?” The Master told him of the state he had experienced during the walk, item by item. The hermit gravely cautioned him: “You are still within the state of the form aggregate; this is not your original mind-nature. I have lived here for more than thirty years, and apart from nights of rain, snow, and wind, every night's walking brings such a state. If you do not dwell upon this state, it will not delude your original mind-nature!” The Master deeply trusted his instruction and respectfully made obeisance in thanks.

Meanwhile, Master Miaofeng had already obtained the Buddhist canon and asked Wang Boyu where Master Hanshan had gone. Wang Boyu sent men up Panshan to search for him. Finding him at the crag, they conveyed Master Miaofeng's eagerness to see him. The Master reflected that he had already stayed long in the crag at Panshan, and since he had a prior appointment with Master Miaofeng, he could not but go. When the Master took leave of the hermit, neither could bear the parting. The hermit saw the Master out of the mountains with tears glistening on his face, and did not turn back until he had accompanied him halfway down the slope.

blocks.text: 2. The Bodhisattva Who Holds the Earth

inline.s: (The original text appears in the Chronological Autobiography of Venerable Master Xuyun.)
In the jiachen year, the thirtieth year of the Guangxu reign, I, Master Xuyun, was sixty-five.

In spring, the dharma protectors and the monk Qimin of Guihua Monastery earnestly requested that I come out of retreat (I was then in seclusion) to expound the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment and the Sūtra of Forty-two Sections at the monastery; more than three thousand people took refuge. In autumn, Venerable Mengfo invited me to the Qiong(
qióng

)zhu Monastery to expound the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. There the Śūraṅgama Sūtra and Hanshan's Poems were printed, the woodblocks being kept at the monastery. He also asked me to transmit the precepts. When that was done, the Military Governor of Dali, Zhang Songlin, and Military Governor Li Fuxing, leading the officials and gentry, welcomed me to the prefecture of Dali, where I stayed at Chongsheng Monastery of the Three Pagodas. They asked me to expound the Lotus Sūtra, and again several thousand people took refuge.
[Military Governor (junmen)] An honorific in the Qing dynasty for a regional commander who also held the rank of provincial military commander.

Military Governor Li wished to keep me at Chongsheng Monastery, but I said: ‘I do not dwell in cities. I have long had the vow to lodge at Mount Jizu, but the hereditary temples on the mountain would not allow it. If you protectors can find a piece of land for building a monastery, I am willing to open the halls and receive the assembly, so as to rescue the monastic community of Yunnan and restore the bodhimaṇḍa of Kāśyapa — this is my wish.’ Everyone approved, and Military Governor Li instructed the magistrate of Binchuan County to arrange the matter. In the mountains they found a dilapidated cloister named the Alms-bowl Hermitage, and there I stayed. Though I had no house to live in and no stored grain for meals, still the fourfold assembly of the ten directions (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās) who came were all received by me with courtesy.
[Mount Jizu] Located northwest of Binchuan County in Yunnan Province and northeast of Lake Erhai. Its main peak, Jinding, rises

meters. The mountain is a place of strange jutting peaks, dense forests, wondrous caves, and beautiful scenery. It is one of the ten famous Buddhist mountains and is the bodhimaṇḍa of the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa. [To lodge (guadan)] For a monk to stay overnight at a monastery, also called “hanging up the robes” (guada,
dā

). [Hereditary temple] A small temple. One of the forms of temple in our country, distinguished from the larger “monasteries of the ten directions.” Such temples are generally the private property of a single monk or a line of monks, and their property may be disposed of at will by the incumbent — unlike the monasteries of the ten directions, which are held in common by the whole saṅgha. [Upāsaka] Translated into Chinese as “pure-faith gentleman,” a male lay follower who in home life draws near to and serves the Three Jewels and upholds the five precepts. [Upāsikā] Translated as “pure-faith lady,” a female lay follower who in home life draws near to and serves the Three Jewels and upholds the five precepts.

Since the Jiaqing reign, no one had lived in the Alms-bowl Hermitage, because to the right of its main gate stood a huge rock — a “white tiger” inauspicious influence, most unlucky. I planned to dig a pond there for releasing living beings, in order to alter the geomantic configuration. I hired workmen to break the rock up, but it would not shatter, so we dug away the earth to inspect it: it had no root. The great rock was nine chi and four cun high and seven chi and six cun wide, flat on top, so that one could sit on it in full lotus. I then contracted laborers to move it twenty-eight zhang to the left. More than a hundred workmen came and labored with all their strength for three days, but could not move it, and went away regardless. I then prayed to the sangharama (the dharma-protecting deity), recited the Buddha's mantra, and, leading a dozen or so monks, moved the great rock twenty-eight zhang to the left. This caused a great stir, and crowds gathered to watch, amazed that the gods had lent their aid. Some busybody titled it “the Cloud-moved Rock,” and many scholars wrote poems upon it; I too composed a poem to record the event.
[Jiaqing] The reign title of Emperor Renzong of the Qing (Aisin Gioro Yongyan) (C.E.
). [Sitting in full lotus (jiafu,
jiā fū

)] The seated posture of a meditator: with both feet crossed and placed upon the opposite thighs, it is called “full lotus”; with only the left foot pressing the right thigh, or only the right foot pressing the left thigh, it is called “half lotus.”

I planned to rebuild the monastery on the old site of the Alms-bowl Hermitage so as to receive the monastic assembly of the ten directions. To start the work, funds were urgently needed. So I left Master Jiechen to manage internal affairs and went alone to Tengchong to beg alms. From Xiaguan to Yongchang, the road passes a place called Hemu. For several hundred li the road there is rough and difficult, and officials and commoners alike had never repaired it. The local people said that a monk from another province had made a vow to repair the road through austere practice, never soliciting donations but letting passers-by help with his food; for several decades he had never wavered. Thanks to his repairs, the road was nine-tenths passable. The people of Pupiao were deeply grateful and wished to build a monastery of the Peacock Wisdom King and invite him to be its abbot. He was unwilling, caring only to repair the road. When I heard of this I was quite astonished, and so I pressed on along the road.

At dusk we met on the road, and I saw him returning with a hoe over his shoulder and a winnowing basket in his hand. I went up to greet him, but he glared at me without speaking. Paying no heed, I followed him to his temple. When I saw him set down his hoe and sit on the meditation cushion, I went forward and made obeisance. He neither looked at me nor uttered a sound, so I sat down facing him and meditated. The next morning he cooked, and I tended the fire for him. When the food was ready he did not call me, so I took my bowl and served myself. After the meal, he shouldered the hoe and I carried the basket, and together we moved stones, dug mud, and spread sand. Thus we sat together and worked together for more than ten days, without his saying a single word — each leaving the other in peace.

One night the moon was as bright as day, and I sat in full lotus on a great rock outside the temple, not returning even late into the night. He stepped lightly to my back and shouted: ‘What are you doing here?’ I opened my eyes slightly and answered slowly: ‘Looking at the moon.’
He asked: ‘Where is the moon?’
I answered: ‘What fine rosy light.’
He said: ‘Fish eyes are many, and hard to tell from pearls — do not mistake a rainbow's glow for rosy clouds.’
I said: ‘The light enfolds the myriad forms, timeless and free; it belongs to neither yin nor yang, and no obstruction can veil it.’
Grasping my hand, he laughed heartily and said: ‘The night is deep; please return to the temple to rest.’

The next day we conversed joyfully. He said he was ‘a native of Xiangtan, named Chanxiu. I left home in my youth, and at twenty-four, in the meditation hall of Jinshan, I gained a place of rest. Later I made pilgrimage to Tibet and returned to China by way of Burma. Seeing this road rough and hard for men and horses to travel, and moved by the holy deeds of the Bodhisattva Who Holds the Earth in ages past, I have repaired the road here alone for several decades. I am now eighty-three and have never met a true friend. Today I am fortunate to meet one of karmic affinity, and for the first time I can pour out what is in my heart.’ I also told him the causes of my own leaving home. The next day, after breakfast, I took my leave of him, and we parted with great laughter.
[Gain a place of rest] Chan Master Weixin of Qingyuan said:
“Thirty years ago, before this old monk had investigated Chan, I saw mountains as mountains and waters as waters. Later, when I personally met a
(good)

spiritual friend and gained an entrance, I saw mountains as not mountains and waters as not waters. Now that I have gained a place of rest, I once again see mountains simply as mountains and waters simply as waters.”

[The Bodhisattva Who Holds the Earth] The Bodhisattva Who Holds the Earth awakened through “earth” to the way of leveling the ground of the mind and attained perfect penetration through the element of earth. The primary cause of this bodhisattva's cultivation was first to level the outer “earth” (

“The Bodhisattva Who Holds the Earth rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and said to the Buddha: I recall that in ages past, when the Tathāgata Universal Light appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu who, at all important roads, ferries, fields, and dangerous passes, wherever the ground was unsuitable and obstructed or harmed carts and horses, would level and fill it, sometimes building bridges and sometimes carrying sand and earth. Thus I toiled through the appearances of countless Buddhas in the world.”

), and later, following the teaching of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, leveled the mind inwardly, reaching the state where both mind and earth are level, and thereby realized perfect penetration. (See the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.)
